elements.note: The god-name most used in Norse names; on its own it gave only Þórir and Þóra.
As a second element it was usually said -ólfr; Cleasby-Vigfusson links Ulpha and Ulverston in north England to it.
Bjǫrn and Bjarni were common names on their own.
Shortened to -kell at the end of names; Cleasby-Vigfusson links its popularity to the holy cauldron used at sacrifices.
Old Norse also had the shorter word ari, 'eagle', mostly in poetry.
Before r it became Ást-, as in Ástríðr; Cleasby-Vigfusson thinks Ás- in names may point to Thor.
Very common at the end of women's names; rare as a first element in Norse.
A poetic word; older form guðr.
In names it usually appears without the r, as Sig-.
Not the English word hall: as a name element it means a stone.
Whether the Ei- of Eiríkr means 'ever' or 'one' is disputed.
Ormr was also a name on its own, and the name of King Olaf Tryggvason's longship Ormr inn Langi.
Used as a man's name on its own; Haukadalr is an Icelandic place.
Common at the end of Icelandic women's names; in poetry it can simply mean a woman.
Women's name ending; not the same word as friðr, 'peace'.
Uncertain: Cleasby-Vigfusson says Vé- in names may be vé 'home, sanctuary' or a separate word for 'holy'.
Uncertain: the word means both 'firebrand' and 'sword blade', and it is unclear which is meant in names.
Uncertain: probably from gríma, 'mask, hood', and one of Odin's names, but the origin is not settled.
Usually shortened to Ragn- or Rǫgn- in names.
The v drops in Haraldr and Ingjaldr.
Sveinn began as a byname and became a very common name; English swain comes from the same word.
Mostly at the end of women's names.

elements.meaning: Yngvi, a name of the god Freyr
elements.note: Cleasby-Vigfusson notes Ingi- names were especially popular among the early Swedes.
In some names Guð- may come instead from guðr, 'battle' (Wiktionary on Guðrún).
In names it usually appears as -varðr.
Often worn down in names: Hrólfr is the Norse match of Rudolph.
A women's name ending; it became -borg in Swedish and Danish, as in Ingeborg.
Svanr was also a man's name on its own.
Not a frequent element, says Cleasby-Vigfusson.
Also spelt bœr; the -by names of northern and eastern England mark Norse and Danish settlement.
Very common in Danish names (-trup, -rup); in England it gave -thorp and -thorpe.
Cleasby-Vigfusson notes it in northern England (Ormathwaite, Langthwaite) but never in Icelandic place-names.
Spelt toft as well as topt in old Norse writing.
Cleasby-Vigfusson compares Langdale, Borrowdale and Wensleydale to Icelandic dale names.
Became firth in Scotland and -ford in Irish names; English ford is related but not the same word.
Not every British -wick is Norse: inland ones come from Latin vicus through Old English.
In Iceland it was also used of waterside meadows cut off by ditches.
The Norse often called the Northern and Western Isles simply Eyjar, 'the Isles'.

elements.meaning: ravine, narrow glen with a stream
elements.note: Survives as gill or ghyll in place-names of northern England and Scotland.
In Iceland fell was a single hill and fjall a mountain; northern English fell comes from the Norse.
Rare in Iceland, where lækr was the usual word; common in northern England as beck.
Northern English how comes from it; Norse farms often had a mound from which the owner could view his land.
Cleasby-Vigfusson links some Icelandic groves to worship and says Lund in northern England marks Norse settlement.
The same root as English yard and garden.
Norwegian sæter; also spelt setr.
First a hut put up for temporary use, like a shieling; later also a hall.
Survives as keld, 'a spring', in northern English.
English skerry comes from it.
Related to English moor and mire; common in Icelandic place-names such as Mýrar.
Tynwald is still the name of the Isle of Man's parliament; Dingwall's origin is called probable.
Kirkwall's -wall is a later reshaping of -vágr.
Niðaróss is the old name of Trondheim in Norway.
Norse sources called Stamford Bridge Stanfurðubryggja; Scots brigg is related.
